hpi_details: 24-month-old male brought in by parents for speech delay. He currently says only 3 words ('mama', 'papa', 'water'), but understands simple commands and points to show things. He has good eye contact, plays pretend with toys, and walked at 13 months, indicating normal social and motor development. Parents report a history of recurrent ear infections over the past year (5 episodes) and note he sometimes does not respond when called from another room. Screen time is reported at 3 hours a day.
ideas: parents wonder if his heavy screen time or frequent ear infections are causing the speech delay
concerns: parents worried he might have autism or a permanent learning disability
expectations: want a hearing test and a referral to a speech therapist to help him catch up
pmh: Recurrent acute otitis media (5 episodes in the past year).
social_hx: Lives with parents. Screen time is 3 hours a day.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Bilingual households may have a temporary silent period, but total vocabulary size across all languages should still meet milestones.
Children with profound hearing loss or structural airway anomalies require more urgent and specialized multidisciplinary intervention.
common_misconceptions: Assuming speech delay is always an early sign of autism, ignoring normal social reciprocity and pretend play.
Reassuring parents that 'boys talk late' without arranging a formal hearing assessment.
Delaying speech-language therapy referral until the child is older.
Failing to ask about screen time and environmental interactive stimulation.
core_concepts: Language delay in toddlers must be evaluated across all domains (receptive, expressive, social/pragmatic) to differentiate isolated delay from global developmental delay or autism spectrum disorder.
Recurrent acute otitis media is a major risk factor for otitis media with effusion, which can cause fluctuating conductive hearing loss and subsequent speech delay.
Hearing assessment (formal audiology) is mandatory for any child presenting with speech or language delay.
Early intervention with speech-language therapy and environmental modifications (reducing screen time, increasing interactive talk/reading) significantly improves outcomes.
dangerous_errors: Failing to evaluate for hearing loss in a child with speech delay and a history of recurrent ear infections.
Missing red flags for autism spectrum disorder, such as poor eye contact, lack of pointing, or loss of previously acquired skills.
Overlooking the negative impact of excessive screen time on early language development.
diagnostic_clues: Key HPI features: 24-month-old saying only 3 words, but has normal receptive language (understands commands) and normal social skills (good eye contact, pointing, pretend play). History of recurrent ear infections and intermittent lack of response to name when called from another room.
Objective/Exam findings: Typical findings would include dull, retracted tympanic membranes with decreased mobility, suggestive of middle ear effusion. Normal neurologic and interactive play exam.
Relevant background/PMH: Recurrent acute otitis media (5 episodes in the past year).
management_principles: Perform a formal audiology assessment to rule out conductive hearing loss from otitis media with effusion.
Refer to Pediatric ENT if hearing loss or chronic middle ear effusion is confirmed.
Refer for Speech-Language Therapy evaluation and early intervention services.
Advise parents to reduce screen time to less than 1 hour per day and increase interactive reading and talking.
Complete the national infant health screening developmental questionnaire to formally screen all domains.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Expressive language delay and conductive hearing loss secondary to otitis media with effusion in toddlers

reference_soap.assessment: Expressive language delay, likely secondary to conductive hearing loss from recurrent otitis media with effusion. No signs of autism spectrum disorder (normal social/pragmatic development).
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: WNL. Gen: Alert, active, interactive toddler. HEENT: Tympanic membranes dull, retracted, with decreased mobility bilaterally suggestive of middle ear effusion. Neuro: Normal tone and strength, normal gait. Psych: Makes good eye contact, responds to gestures, engages in imaginative play with blocks during visit.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Referral for formal audiology evaluation to assess for hearing loss. 2. ENT referral for possible tympanostomy tubes if persistent effusion is confirmed. 3. Refer to early intervention for speech-language therapy. 4. Counsel parents to reduce screen time to <1 hour/day and increase face-to-face interactive play. 5. Complete the national infant health screening developmental questionnaire.
reference_soap.subjective: 24-month-old boy brought by parents due to speech delay. Currently says only 3 words ('mama', 'papa', 'water'). Follows simple commands, points to objects, maintains good eye contact, and engages in pretend play. Walked at 13 months. History of 5 ear infections in the past year. Sometimes ignores parents when called from another room. Screen time is 3 hours daily.

learning_objectives: Conduct a structured developmental history assessing expressive, receptive, and social/pragmatic domains to characterize speech delay.
Identify recurrent acute otitis media and excessive screen time as key risk factors for expressive language delay.
Recognize the importance of mandatory hearing assessment in any child presenting with speech or language delay.
Differentiate isolated expressive language delay from autism spectrum disorder by confirming normal eye contact, pointing, and pretend play.

teaching.diagnosis: Expressive language delay with possible conductive hearing loss

must_ask.say: How many words can he say clearly, and does he put two words together?
Can he follow simple instructions, like 'give me the ball' without you pointing?

must_ask.objective: Screen for autism red flags (social domains)
must_ask.say: Does he make good eye contact, point to things he wants, and play pretend with his toys?

must_ask.objective: Assess hearing and middle ear disease history
must_ask.say: Does he ever seem to have trouble hearing you, and has he had frequent ear infections?
How much time does he spend watching TV, phones, or tablets each day?
We must arrange a formal hearing test first, as fluid in his ears may be making it hard for him to hear and learn words.
I will also refer him to a speech therapist and suggest completing the national infant health screening questionnaire.

teaching.one_liner: 24-month-old boy with normal social and motor milestones presenting with expressive speech delay, heavy screen time, and a history of recurrent ear infections.
red_flags: Lack of pointing or sharing interest
Loss of previously acquired language or social skills

history.answer: He is two years old now, but he hardly speaks any words yet, so we brought him in to get checked.
Around when he turned 18 months old, my spouse and I noticed he was not picking up words like other kids his age.
At his routine checkups his height and weight have always tracked right along the 50th percentile, and he is growing steadily.
He was born at 39 weeks weighing 3.2 kilograms without any complications, and he went home with us two days later.
He eats three balanced meals a day with a hearty appetite, drinks whole milk, and has never had trouble chewing or swallowing.
He has never had chronic diarrhea, blood in his stool, shortness of breath, turning blue, or urinary troubles.
He does not have headaches, vomiting, vision issues, excessive thirst, excessive urination, cold intolerance, or sluggishness.
He held his head up at 3 months, sat alone at 7 months, walked independently at 13 months, and feeds himself with a spoon.
He currently says only three words, which are 'mama', 'papa', and 'water'. He does not put two words together yet.
He understands simple spoken requests like 'bring me the ball' or 'come here' when he is looking right at us.
He makes wonderful eye contact with us, smiles back when smiled at, and points his finger to show us things he finds interesting.
He loves pretending to feed his stuffed bear or rolling toy cars across the floor, and he does not repeat hand-flapping or spinning.
He passed his newborn hearing test, but he had five separate ear infections over the past year, and he sometimes ignores us when called from another room.
No, he has never lost any words, motor skills, or social abilities that he once had.
We both work normal hours, but he watches television cartoons or tablet videos for about 3 hours every day.
We wonder whether watching too much tablet screen time or having so many ear infections might be delaying his speech.
We are terrified that he might have autism spectrum disorder or a permanent learning disability.
We would really like to get his hearing properly checked and get a referral to a speech therapist so he can catch up.
Aside from the five bouts of middle ear infections during this past year, he has had no major illnesses.
He has never had any operations and has never been admitted to a hospital.
He is not taking any prescription medications, vitamins, or over-the-counter syrups right now.
He has no known allergies to medicines, foods, or environmental triggers.
Neither of us smokes, and our home is completely smoke-free.
There is no alcohol or substance use anywhere in our household.
He lives in an apartment with both parents, and his mother stays home to care for him during the day.
Both parents are average height, and there is no family history of speech delay, hearing loss, autism, or genetic conditions.
All of his childhood immunizations are completely up to date according to the national schedule.
He does not go to daycare or preschool yet, so he stays home with his mother every day.

exam.finding: Temperature is 36.9°C, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.

Height is 87 cm at the 50th percentile, weight is 12.3 kg at the 50th percentile, and head circumference is 48.5 cm at the 50th percentile, showing steady proportional growth along normal percentiles.
Alert, active, interactive toddler in no acute distress, with normal body proportions and no dysmorphic facial features.
Both tympanic membranes are dull and retracted with decreased mobility and amber fluid visible, consistent with middle ear effusion; no erythema or perforation.
Turns inconsistently to soft conversational speech or rustling sounds presented from behind, but responds promptly to visual gestures.
Nasal mucosa is pink without rhinorrhea, and oral examination shows a normal palate, intact uvula, and normal tonsils without erythema.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds, and no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal respiratory effort and no wheezing, crackles, or stridor.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended, with no palpable hepatosplenomegaly or abdominal masses.
Normal muscle bulk and symmetric active movements across all four limbs, with normal age-appropriate muscle tone.
Walks independently with a steady, normal toddler gait, climbs easily onto the chair, and demonstrates normal balance.
Maintains warm eye contact, responds to maternal gestures, points to pictures in a book, and engages in imaginative pretend play with toy blocks.
